chapter_theme: Songs at Kodainagar (கோடைநகர்): two twin songs trace a life from the womb through play, women and the search for wealth to the edge of hell, two short akam songs plead for a lovesick girl, one catalogues the brutes who fall into Yama's pit, and others ask for the feet at the hour of death and for the yogic stilling of breath that ends dying.
structure_note: 703 and 704 are twins, in the same metre and with the same closing plea. 705 and 706 are akam songs in another voice. 707 has no plea at all, only a list of sinners and their end. 708 is a death song and 709 a yogic one.

703.reading: The poet tells his life from the first day as an embryo in his mother's body, born with desire, raised with love, grown into a handsome man who played, roamed the earth, mixed with women and sought wealth thinking it needful, and asks to be given love to reach the flower feet before he falls into ruinous hell. The praise names Murugan nephew of Narayana who killed Ravana for carrying off Sita, son of the one whom gods, sages, Vishnu and Brahma could not find in their search, and the lord who came to dwell at Kodainagar.
703.nuance: The plea is a life in stages (ஆகமலமாகி நின்று, பிறந்து, வளர்ந்து, ஆளழகனாகி, மாதருடனே கலந்து, பொருள்தேடி), each a step toward the hell it ends in. What it asks for is love (அன்பு) that reaches the feet, not release as such. கோதைமலை in the praise is unclear to me.

704.reading: A twin of 703: the poet tells of lying long in the woman's body, coming to earth in pains near death, the birth rites, crying, crawling and playing, being called a child, then lying on the heavy breasts of sweet-voiced women, seeking wealth and wandering, and asks for love to reach the one flower foot before he falls into hell. The praise names Siva who drank the poison as nectar, Narayana who answered the elephant's cry of 'Root' in the pond, Valli whose lips' nectar Murugan drank, and the vel that felled Sura, at Kodainagar.
704.nuance: சாதகமுமான பின்பு: the birth rite (jatakarma) is one stage among the others. The elephant crying மூலமே is the story of Gajendra, as in 25.

705.reading: A short akam song in the voice of someone pleading for a lovesick girl: Kama, who did not die though the rider of the bull burned him to ash, wounds her with his fragrant arrows, and the flute with its seven-note holes torments her; it asks Murugan not to let this deer-like girl, wasting into enmity, hurt, end and longing, perish, but to come, look on her and join her, or else give his unfading kadamba garland. The praise names the Kumara of the peacock who circles the fourteen worlds, the deathless, ageless lord of Kodai, who fought until great Sura fell uprooted, the hero of the vel.
705.nuance: The song is a chain of short rhyming words (வாராய் பாராய் சேராய்; தேவா சாவா மூவா நாதா), so the splitting is often a guess. Asking for the god's garland when he will not come is a standing akam motif of the Thiruppugazh. I read the voice as a mother's or companion's; it is not said.

706.reading: A short akam song: a lovesick girl, or one speaking for her, asks Murugan to come and embrace her with his twelve arms so that she does not perish from the sea that roars around the world, the slander the women speak each day, and the moon that burns like poison. The praise names the chest that embraced the hunter girl, the peacock hero who stands at Kodai, and the lord who pierced the mountain so that Death took fright and loosed the fetters of the gods.
706.nuance: The torments are the classical ones: the sea's roar, the town's gossip (வஞ்சியர் உற்று உரைக்கும் வசை) and the moon that burns like the poison (ஆலம்). The speaker is not named.

707.reading: The song lists the brutes (குண்டர்கள்) who fall into the pit where Yama torments: those who make friends and then betray, who forget the good done them, who break their vows, who revile the great, who obstruct giving when they see it, who abandon their oaths, who long to live forever, who wreck justice and dharma, who swell with pride, who suffer in maya, and who seize the property of the gods. The praise names Rama, whose arrow pierced the seven trees and Vali and brought down Ravana's Lanka, as uncle, Murugan of Vayalur with its towers and peacocks, and the lord of Kodai praised by gods and devotees.
707.nuance: There is no plea and no confession: this is a moral catalogue in the manner of the didactic books, and Yama's pit is its only sanction. ஈவது கண்டு தகைந்த, blocking another's giving, and ஓதிய நன்றி மறந்த, forgetting a good done, are Kural sins. வயலூரா in the praise names another shrine.

708.reading: The poet pictures the kin who gather weeping, Yama come with his terrible heavy trident and noose, the bier and the fire, and asks that he not perish thus in ruin but that Murugan, in grace, set him, a man in bonds, at the golden feet. The praise names the vel that fought until Sura fled into the sea, the hero who gave a garland to the honey-girl in the forest, the one who goes singing at Koodal, and the lord of Kodai with its rice fields and groves.
708.nuance: பாசத்தேனை: the poet calls himself the one in bonds, so Yama's noose (பாசம்) and his own bondage share a word. கூடற் பாடிக் கோவைப் பாவைக் கூடப் பாடித் திரிவோனே may refer to Murugan singing at Madurai, or to a kovai poem; I can't identify it.

709.reading: The poet asks whether, with the bindu that read books and argued creeds cannot give made steady as the light of truth, and the breath that runs in the nose turned into the hall of the skull, he will not by yogic samadhi end this dying again and again in a world crowded by the demon of delusion, the life leaving through every pore. The praise names the vel that dried the sea and frightened Brahma, the potter of the Vedas, the Murugan who, dazed by Kama's five arrows, fell at the hunter girl's feet, the son of the destroyer of the cities, and the lord of the cock banner who came to dwell at Kodai.
709.nuance: A rare yogic plea: knowledge from books and sects (வாசித்த நூல் மதங்கள்) is set against the bindu-light, and the breath is to be turned (மடைமாறி) into the skull (கபால மன்றில்). The middle lines (யோசித்த யாருடம்பை நேசித்துறாது அலைந்து) are hard to divide, and whether the dying through the pores is ordinary death or the yogi's departure is not clear.

links.note: Twin songs in one metre: both walk a life from the womb through childhood, women and the hunt for wealth, and both end in the same plea for love that reaches the feet before one falls into hell. 704 dwells longer on infancy (the birth rite, crawling), 703 on youth and roaming.
Both condemn the man who begrudges another's giving: the Kural says his kin will be left without food or clothing, and 707 puts him among those who fall into Yama's pit.
The Kural says there is no escape for one who kills a good done to him; 707 lists those who forget the good done them among the brutes who fall into Yama's pit, giving that 'no escape' a place.

Both make the stilled and turned breath the end of dying: Tirumular says that when breath stays with the mind there is no birth or death, and 709 asks that, with the breath turned into the skull and samadhi gained, the endless dying cease.

Both songs trace one life from the womb to ruin: 195 from rolling in blood in a woman's body (உதிரமதிலே உருண்டு) through sixteen years to the women's nets and the wealth lost, 703 from the first day in the mother's body (ஆதிமுதல் நாளில் என்றன் தாயுடலில்) through youth, women and the search for wealth (பொருள்தேடி). 195 asks grace to rule him, 703 asks for love (அன்பு) that reaches the feet before hell; the pairing shows the life-confession as a set form in distant parts of the book.

705 names among the girl's torments the flute with its seven-note holes (ஏழோசைத் தொளையாலே), beside Kama's fragrant arrows. Kural 1228 calls the herdsman's flute a weapon that kills (ஆயன் குழல்போலும் கொல்லும் படை). Both turn the flute's music into a weapon against the lovesick; in 705 the bamboo (வேய்) is named in a run of rhyming words that is hard to divide.

706 asks Murugan to come lest the girl perish from the sea's roar, the slander the women speak each day (நாளும் வஞ்சியர் உற்று உரைக்கும் வசை) and the moon that burns like poison. Kural 1147 says the town's gossip (ஊரவர் கௌவை) is the manure on which this sickness grows. Both make gossip feed the love-sickness rather than shame it away; the song can only ask the god to end it by coming.

708 pictures the kin who gather weeping (சூழ்துற்றார் துற்றழுவாரும்), Yama with trident and noose, the bier and the fire (பாடைக் கூடத் தீயில்). Tirumanthiram 157 follows the wailing kin, wives and children only to the edge of the town (ஊர்த்துறைக் காலே ஒழிவர்), then the wood, the fire and the bath. Tirumular shows how far the kin go; 708 turns the same scene into a plea to be set at the golden feet (பொற்பாதத்தே வைத்தருள்வாயே).

source_issues: Song 703: unflagged garble பாழவெளநேரகெய் தாம (line 7); the twin song 704 has பாழ்நரகெய் தாம, so read பாழ்நரகு எய்தாமல்.
Song 707: corrupt character in வயலு¡ரா (line 21), clearly வயலூரா; also சொங்கள் (line 11) may be a garble for சொம்கள் or சொத்துகள், 'property'.
